rationale:
Does a `calls` edge lose a receiver that the source states? `Mojo::IOLoop->start` names a CLASS, so the method's owner is derivable and the target is `IOLoop.start`. The lane emitted the bare leaf `start`, which is a precision loss and not a cosmetic one: `Mojo::IOLoop->remove`, `Mojo::IOLoop->stream` and `Mojo::IOLoop->server` all collapsed onto `remove`, `stream` and `server`, so two classes' same-named methods became one node in the graph and a caller of one looked like a caller of the other. Measured with script/m14/tmp/perl-receiver-scope.mts: 10,781 method-call SITES across the seven corpora had a provable package receiver, and 4,800 more had a bare bareword that is a VARIABLE and must keep the leaf. Neither the differential nor any other fixture could see this, because the oracle derived the target by leaf name exactly as the analyzer did — the third time this pair has agreed on a shared premise, after the `use constant { ... }` dead branch and the oracle's `!inSub` gap. So the number came from the AST.

There is deliberately NO forbid on the bare leaf `start`, even though that is the pre-fix shape for line 4, because line 6 legitimately emits that same leaf. The harness matches a relationship by type/from/target and cannot tell which line produced it, so forbidding it here would forbid the correct answer for the variable receiver. The pre-fix shape is covered instead by the expectation on `IOLoop.start` and by the perl/receiver-qualification-dropped mutant.

The rule is ONE rule with two labels, and every line pins a different part of it:

  line 4   Mojo::IOLoop->start      class receiver  -> QUALIFIED  IOLoop.start
  line 5   Mojo::Util->encode_json  class receiver  -> QUALIFIED  Util.encode_json
  line 6   app->start               DIRECT bare bareword, no `::` -> leaf  start
  line 7   $loop->remove           value receiver  -> leaf        remove
  line 8   $self->helper           value receiver  -> leaf        helper
  line 9   app->log->level         `app` is a LEXICAL holding a server -> leaf  level
  line 10  Mojo::IOLoop->reset      `reset` is a PERL BUILTIN -> nothing at all
  line 11  $self->${\( ... )}      the METHOD is COMPUTED, not written -> no edge,
                                   but the real call INSIDE it is still published

Line 6 is the load-bearing one, and getting it right took a second attempt. The first draft pinned only `app->log->level` on the theory that it was the obvious shape — but the DIRECT invocant there is the CALL `app->log`, not the bareword, so `namesAClass` is false on it and even the naive over-correction would not have qualified it. That forbid pin was dead: it could never fire. The shape the corpora actually contain is a bare bareword as the DIRECT invocant — mojo's examples/chat.pl:22, hello.pl:8, hello-template.pl:8 and proxy.pl:20 are all `app->start`, and Mojo::Base.pm:101 is `feature->import(':5.16')`. Line 6 is that shape, and deleting the `::` proof from the analyzer turns its forbid red, which is how it was verified.

Line 10 is the case that stops qualification from defeating the builtin set: `addCall` tests its argument against PERL_BUILTINS, and when the argument became the qualified `IOLoop.reset` the test missed `reset` — a builtin — so this line emitted an edge for a builtin. The builtin test is about the METHOD, and both reasons live in the code.

Line 11 is the seventh shape, and the only one whose ABSENCE is the point. A symbolic deref — `$self->${\( EXPR \)}` — is perl's "call the method this expression computes", so the METHOD NAME IS NOT WRITTEN anywhere in the file. The grammar hands the whole expression to the `method` field, and the lane used to publish that text as a callee name: measured `calls -> DemolishAll->new` (Moo/Object.pm:56, a `function` field holding compound text) and `calls -> ${\( $tc->can('coercion')||sub { ... } )}` (Moo/Role.pm:224). Those are not weaker claims, they are FABRICATED ones — a target that is not written cannot be verified against the source by the line oracle at all. So no edge is emitted for the deref, and the rule is a POSITIVE allowlist on the callee text rather than a "does this look wrong" test, because a negative test only ever enumerates the dynamic cases somebody already hit.

The control is the second half: the `Moo::IOLoop->next_tick` INSIDE the expression is a perfectly ordinary class call and is published as `IOLoop.next_tick`. Refusing the deref must not swallow the real code around it, and a fixture that only asserted the absence would pass against an analyzer that had simply stopped walking.

expectRelationships.note: a receiver that is a `package`-bearing bareword is a PROVABLE class, so the owner is derivable and the target carries it
`Mojo::Util` leaf-qualifies to `Util`, the same convention the `instantiates` path already used for `Util.constructor`

`app` is a DIRECT bare bareword, and the shape the corpora really contain. A lexical holding a Mojo::Server, not a class, so the leaf is correct. This is the pin that stands between the narrow rule and the naive `namesAClass` one.
a VALUE receiver has no class to name, so the leaf is the honest target and this is the control for the two lines above
the CHAINED form of the same variable receiver. Kept because it is common, but it is a weaker pin than line 6: the direct invocant is the call, so this row would not catch the naive rule on its own.
the CONTROL for the line above: a real class call written inside a symbolic deref is still published. Refusing to name the computed method must not cost the code around it.

forbidRelationships.note: the over-correction: a bare bareword qualified as if it were a class, inventing a type named `app` for a lexical. Verified to fire — removing the `::` proof from the analyzer turns this row red.
the same over-correction on the chained form. A second forbid, and a weaker one for the reason given on the line 9 expectation.
there is no `remove` on a class receiver here; `$loop->remove` is a value receiver and keeps the leaf

`reset` is a perl BUILTIN. The first version of the fix qualified the target BEFORE addCall's builtin test, so the test saw `IOLoop.reset` instead of `reset` and stopped suppressing it. The builtin test is about the method being invoked, never about the shape of the edge's target.

perl/symbolic-deref-callee-published-as-a-name: a callee rebuilt from code text rather than written in the file. Named by SUFFIX because the fabricated target IS the code, so no exact name is stable to pin - which is the point.

forbidSymbols.name: app
forbidSymbols.note: `app` is a receiver in a method call, not a declaration in this file; a class symbol here would mean the analyzer had decided a lexical was a package

expectUniqueIds.name: run
expectUniqueIds.note: the method `run` and the class `RQ` must not collapse onto one id, or the calls edges above would be emitted from the wrong node
